title: A Dominican day at home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disputation: the objections first, stated fairly, then the answer, then a reply to every one. Your line was a good question. Whose best point did you say back to them? Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

No friary. No white habit. No bell in a cloister calling anyone to choir. Just a kitchen, a phone on the counter, a commute, a shift, dinner, and dishes. For these last weeks we've followed the Dominicans: an innkeeper up all night, nuns before friars, a motto of truth, a climber in Turin, a theologian who waited, a painter's quiet walls, a founder's last promise. Today is the last day with them, and it asks a small question. Could an ordinary day, in an ordinary house, have the Dominican shape? Not a monastery schedule. Just three motions, fitted around the life already there. Today's word is that day.
screen: `NO FRIARY. JUST A KITCHEN.` → `WEEKS WITH THE DOMINICANS.` → `COULD A HOME DAY HAVE THEIR SHAPE?`

segments.voice: Here's the shape, in three motions. Morning: pray. It can be short. A Dominican at home might pray one psalm before the phone comes on. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims gives a line that fits a morning: "O Lord, in the morning thou shalt hear my voice." Morning first, before the day gets its say. Midday: study. One page, chewed slowly. A Gospel passage, a paragraph of the catechism, a few lines of a saint. Remember the friars who went to the university towns: for them, study wasn't a hobby beside prayer, it was prayer with the mind switched on. Evening: share one truth. Not a lecture. One true thing you learned or noticed today, handed to someone: at dinner, in a text, while folding laundry. That's the preacher in the house. Thomas Aquinas, the Dominican teacher, has a phrase for the whole pattern that Dominicans still quote: contemplata aliis tradere, to contemplate, and to hand on to others what you've contemplated. Pray and study fill the cup. Sharing pours it out. If one of the three goes missing, the day tips: all prayer and no sharing turns inward, all sharing and no study runs dry. And that's the Dominican stretch of the path, folded into one ordinary day. Tomorrow a new family arrives, the Jesuits, with a book of their own in hand. But tonight the Dominicans leave you their three motions.
screen: `MORNING: PRAY, BEFORE THE PHONE.` · `MIDDAY: STUDY. ONE PAGE, SLOWLY.` · `EVENING: SHARE ONE TRUE THING.` · `CONTEMPLATE, THEN HAND IT ON.` · then, large: `IN THE MORNING THOU SHALT HEAR MY VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one thing, and choose who you'll share it with. Settle, and breathe. Think back over this stretch of days with the Dominicans and find one thing that stuck: a story, a phrase, a picture. Hold it. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence, as if explaining it to a friend who's never heard of Dominic. Then choose the person who'll hear it today. If you pray, you can ask that it reach them as a gift, not a sermon. The bell holds the time.
A Dominican day at home. Pray in the morning, study at midday, share one true thing at night: the order's rhythm, fitted around an ordinary life. Today's word.
screen: `A DOMINICAN DAY AT HOME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pray, study, share. Today, tell the person you chose your one sentence, then let it go. Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Lay Dominicans and others drawn to the order shape ordinary days around prayer, study and sharing, some praying morning and evening prayer from the Liturgy of the Hours and reading scripture or a spiritual book each day.

notes: Last day of the Dominicans (days 1229–1249): the hook names several of the stretch's days; tomorrow opens the Jesuits.
The hook says 'these last weeks' rather than a count of weeks (claims rule).
'Dominicans still quote' contemplata aliis tradere (sometimes given as a second Dominican motto): confirm wording.
The morning/midday/evening pattern is offered as a home adaptation, not an official Dominican rule.
